source: Reference was made to the historical story of Jonah and the whale in the preceding chapter. Now some Nantucketers rather distrust this historical story of Jonah and the whale. But then there were some sceptical Greeks and Romans, who, standing out from the orthodox pagans of their times, equally doubted the story of Hercules and the whale, and Arion and the dolphin; and yet their doubting those traditions did not make those traditions one whit the less facts, for all that.

One old Sag-Harbor whaleman’s chief reason for questioning the Hebrew story was this:—He had one of those quaint old-fashioned Bibles, embellished with curious, unscientific plates; one of which represented Jonah’s whale with two spouts in his head—a peculiarity only true with respect to a species of the Leviathan (the Right Whale, and the varieties of that order), concerning which the fishermen have this saying, “A penny roll would choke him”; his swallow is so very small. But, to this, Bishop Jebb’s anticipative answer is ready. It is not necessary, hints the Bishop, that we consider Jonah as tombed in the whale’s belly, but as temporarily lodged in some part of his mouth. And this seems reasonable enough in the good Bishop. For truly, the Right Whale’s mouth would accommodate a couple of whist-tables, and comfortably seat all the players. Possibly, too, Jonah might have ensconced himself in a hollow tooth; but, on second thoughts, the Right Whale is toothless.

Another reason which Sag-Harbor (he went by that name) urged for his want of faith in this matter of the prophet, was something obscurely in reference to his incarcerated body and the whale’s gastric juices. But this objection likewise falls to the ground, because a German exegetist supposes that Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a dead whale—even as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents, and crawled into them. Besides, it has been divined by other continental commentators, that when Jonah was thrown overboard from the Joppa ship, he straightway effected his escape to another vessel near by, some vessel with a whale for a figure-head; and, I would add, possibly called “The Whale,” as some craft are nowadays christened the “Shark,” the “Gull,” the “Eagle.” Nor have there been wanting learned exegetists who have opined that the whale mentioned in the book of Jonah merely meant a life-preserver—an inflated bag of wind—which the endangered prophet swam to, and so was saved from a watery doom. Poor Sag-Harbor, therefore, seems worsted all round. But he had still another reason for his want of faith. It was this, if I remember right: Jonah was swallowed by the whale in the Mediterranean Sea, and after three days he was vomited up somewhere within three days’ journey of Nineveh, a city on the Tigris, very much more than three days’ journey across from the nearest point of the Mediterranean coast. How is that?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet within that short distance of Nineveh? Yes. He might have carried him round by the way of the Cape of Good Hope. But not to speak of the passage through the whole length of the Mediterranean, and another passage up the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, such a supposition would involve the complete circumnavigation of all Africa in three days, not to speak of the Tigris waters, near the site of Nineveh, being too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, this idea of Jonah’s weathering the Cape of Good Hope at so early a day would wrest the honor of the discovery of that great headland from Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, and so make modern history a liar.

But all these foolish arguments of old Sag-Harbor only evinced his foolish pride of reason—a thing still more reprehensible in him, seeing that he had but little learning except what he had picked up from the sun and the sea. I say it only shows his foolish, impious pride, and abominable, devilish rebellion against the reverend clergy. For by a Portuguese Catholic priest, this very idea of Jonah’s going to Nineveh via the Cape of Good Hope was advanced as a signal magnification of the general miracle. And so it was. Besides, to this day, the highly enlightened Turks devoutly believe in the historical story of Jonah. And some three centuries ago, an English traveller in old Harris’s Voyages, speaks of a Turkish Mosque built in honor of Jonah, in which Mosque was a miraculous lamp that burnt without any oil.

modern_en.title: Chapter 83 — Jonah Historically Regarded
paragraphs: The last chapter mentioned the historical story of Jonah and the whale. Now, some Nantucketers are rather suspicious of this historical story of Jonah and the whale. But then, there were some skeptical Greeks and Romans who broke ranks with the orthodox pagans of their day and doubted, just as much, the story of Hercules and the whale and that of Arion and the dolphin; and yet their doubts did not make those traditions the slightest bit less factual, for all that.

One old Sag-Harbor whaleman's chief reason for questioning the Hebrew story was this. He had one of those quaint old-fashioned Bibles decorated with curious, unscientific engravings, one of which showed Jonah's whale with two spouts in his head — a peculiarity true only of one species of Leviathan (the Right Whale and the varieties of that order), of which the fishermen have this saying: "A penny roll would choke him"; his swallow is so very small. But Bishop Jebb has an answer to this ready in advance. It is not necessary, the Bishop hints, to think of Jonah as entombed in the whale's belly, but rather as temporarily lodged in some part of his mouth. And this seems reasonable enough of the good Bishop. For truly, the Right Whale's mouth would hold a couple of whist-tables and comfortably seat all the players. Possibly, too, Jonah might have tucked himself away in a hollow tooth; but, on second thought, the Right Whale has no teeth.

Another reason Sag-Harbor (he went by that name) gave for his lack of faith in this matter of the prophet was something vaguely to do with the imprisoned body and the whale's gastric juices. But this objection likewise falls to the ground, because a German biblical interpreter supposes that Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a whale that was already dead — just as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents and crawled inside them. Besides, other continental commentators have guessed that when Jonah was thrown overboard from the Joppa ship, he promptly escaped to another vessel close by, some vessel with a whale for a figurehead; and, I would add, possibly called "The Whale," just as some craft nowadays are christened the "Shark," the "Gull," or the "Eagle." Nor has there been any shortage of learned interpreters who have held that the whale mentioned in the book of Jonah simply meant a life-preserver — an inflated bag of wind — which the endangered prophet swam to, and so was saved from a watery death. Poor Sag-Harbor, then, seems beaten on every side. But he had still another reason for his lack of faith. It was this, if I remember right: Jonah was swallowed by the whale in the Mediterranean Sea, and after three days he was vomited up somewhere within three days' journey of Nineveh, a city on the Tigris, which is very much more than three days' journey from the nearest point of the Mediterranean coast. How is that?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet that close to Nineveh? There was. He could have carried him around by way of the Cape of Good Hope. But leaving aside the voyage through the whole length of the Mediterranean and another up the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, such a theory would mean sailing right around Africa in three days — to say nothing of the fact that the Tigris, near where Nineveh stood, is too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, the idea of Jonah rounding the Cape of Good Hope at such an early date would rob Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, of the honor of finding that great headland, and so make modern history a liar.

Besides, to this day the highly enlightened Turks devoutly believe in the historical story of Jonah. And some three centuries ago, an English traveler in old Harris's Voyages tells of a Turkish mosque built in honor of Jonah, in which there was a miraculous lamp that burned without any oil.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 83 — Jonas historisk betragtet
paragraphs: Det forrige kapitel nævnte den historiske fortælling om Jonas og hvalen. Nu er nogle nantucketere ret mistænksomme over for denne historiske fortælling om Jonas og hvalen. Men dengang var der også nogle skeptiske grækere og romere, som brød med datidens rettroende hedninge og tvivlede lige så meget på fortællingen om Herkules og hvalen og om Arion og delfinen; og alligevel gjorde deres tvivl ikke disse overleveringer det mindste mindre sande for den sags skyld.

Én gammel hvalfanger fra Sag-Harbor havde især denne grund til at tvivle på den hebraiske beretning. Han havde en af de gammeldags, besynderlige bibler, prydet med mærkelige, uvidenskabelige træsnit, og i et af dem havde Jonas' hval to vandstråler i hovedet — noget, der kun passer på én art af Leviatan (rethvalen og de varianter, der hører til dens orden), om hvilken fiskerne har dette ordsprog: »Et rundstykke til en øre ville få ham til at kvæle sig«; så lille er hans svælg. Men biskop Jebb har et svar på det parat på forhånd. Det er ikke nødvendigt, antyder biskoppen, at tænke sig Jonas begravet i hvalens mave, men snarere midlertidigt indlogeret et sted i dens mund. Og det forekommer ganske rimeligt af den gode biskop. For rethvalens mund ville i sandhed kunne rumme et par whist-borde og lade alle spillerne sidde godt. Måske kunne Jonas også have gemt sig i en hul tand; men ved nærmere eftertanke har rethvalen ingen tænder.

En anden grund, som Sag-Harbor (så hed han) gav til sin manglende tro på profeten, var noget utydeligt om det indespærrede legeme og hvalens mavesyre. Men denne indvending falder ligeledes til jorden, fordi en tysk bibeltolker mener, at Jonas må have søgt tilflugt i kroppen af en hval, der allerede var død og drev rundt — ligesom de franske soldater i felttoget i Rusland gjorde deres døde heste til telte og krøb ind i dem. Desuden har andre fastlandskommentatorer gættet på, at da Jonas blev kastet over bord fra skibet fra Joppe, slap han straks over i et andet fartøj tæt ved, et fartøj med en hval som galionsfigur; og jeg vil tilføje, at det måske hed »Hvalen«, ligesom nogle skibe nu om dage døbes »Hajen«, »Mågen« eller »Ørnen«. Og der har heller ikke manglet lærde fortolkere, der har ment, at hvalen i Jonas' bog blot betød en redningskrans — en oppustet luftpose — som den truede profet svømmede hen til og således blev reddet fra at drukne. Stakkels Sag-Harbor ser altså ud til at være slået på alle fronter. Men han havde endnu en grund til sin manglende tro. Den var denne, hvis jeg husker ret: Jonas blev slugt af hvalen i Middelhavet, og efter tre dage blev han spyet op et sted inden for tre dages rejse fra Nineve, en by ved Tigris, som ligger meget mere end tre dages rejse fra det nærmeste punkt på Middelhavets kyst. Hvordan kan det hænge sammen?

Men fandtes der ingen anden måde, hvorpå hvalen kunne sætte profeten i land så tæt på Nineve? Jo. Den kunne have ført ham rundt om Kap det Gode Håb. Men bortset fra rejsen gennem hele Middelhavets længde og endnu en op ad Den Persiske Bugt og Det Røde Hav ville en sådan teori betyde at sejle helt rundt om Afrika på tre dage — for slet ikke at tale om, at Tigris, der hvor Nineve lå, er for lavvandet til, at nogen hval kan svømme i den. Desuden ville tanken om, at Jonas rundede Kap det Gode Håb så tidligt, berøve Bartholomeus Diaz, dets formodede opdager, æren af at have fundet det store forbjerg og dermed gøre den nyere historie til en løgner.

Men alle disse tåbelige indvendinger fra gamle Sag-Harbor viste kun hans tåbelige stolthed over sin fornuft — noget, der var desto mere dadelværdigt hos ham, eftersom han kun havde lidt lærdom ud over det, han havde samlet op af solen og havet. Jeg siger, at det kun viser hans tåbelige, ugudelige stolthed og hans afskyelige, djævelske oprør mod den ærværdige gejstlighed. For en portugisisk katolsk præst fremsatte netop denne tanke om, at Jonas var rejst til Nineve rundt om Kap det Gode Håb, som en bemærkelsesværdig forstørrelse af det almindelige under. Og det var den også. Desuden tror de højtoplyste tyrkere den dag i dag inderligt på den historiske fortælling om Jonas. Og for omkring tre hundrede år siden fortæller en engelsk rejsende i gamle Harris' rejsebeskrivelser om en tyrkisk moské, bygget til ære for Jonas, hvor der var en mirakuløs lampe, som brændte uden olie.
